data.source_text_main_point: Following an FCC investigation into Comcast's data restrictions, major ISPs like Comcast and Time Warner Cable are testing plans to slow speeds or charge extra fees for heavy internet usage, sparking debate over whether these measures unfairly target consumers and prioritize profit over network management.

statements.key_statement: An FCC investigation into Comcast's data restrictions has sparked a congressional debate over how much control internet service providers should have over customer data.
statements.long_statement: The Federal Communications Commission's inquiry into whether Comcast restricted customers from sharing files has ignited a congressional debate regarding the extent of control internet service providers should have over customer data flow, highlighting a growing conflict between regulatory oversight and corporate network management strategies.

statements.key_statement: Comcast will not filter traffic types but still needs to manage the network.
statements.long_statement: Comcast will not filter traffic types but still needs to manage the network.

statements.key_statement: Time Warner Cable will start measuring internet usage and sending invoices for higher speeds and bigger data packages.
statements.long_statement: Time Warner Cable intends to charge customers based on usage levels and speed tiers, operating as a standard utility like an electric provider or mobile carrier, instead of providing unlimited flat-rate internet access.

statements.key_statement: To pay for the infrastructure needed to provide internet access, charging users based on how much data they consume is the most equitable method.
statements.long_statement: Internet service charges based on actual data consumption represent the most equitable method for financing the necessary network upgrades. This approach guarantees that users who download or stream large amounts of information pay their fair share toward building and maintaining the infrastructure.

statements.key_statement: Time Warner Cable's fee-based data plan prioritizes protecting inadequate infrastructure over relieving network congestion.
statements.long_statement: The proposed plan by Time Warner Cable to charge extra fees for heavy data usage functions as a rationing scheme designed to protect an inadequate infrastructure, rather than a strategy intended to relieve network congestion. This approach limits high-definition movie viewing and other essential content, effectively prioritizing the preservation of limited network capacity over meeting consumer demand for faster speeds and larger data allowances.
